utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in this courtroom and just outside the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. An application has been made for the next witness to be called for protective measures. The Chamber was informed that the Defence for Mr. Haradinaj does not object granting the protective measures as requested. I have not heard yet from other Defence counsel. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have no objection; however, I would make a brief comment with regard to those concerns voiced about the Albanian population in the country of domicile. I don't believe it's a valid basis for the granting of any form of measures. But I have no objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- to the measures being granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I have no objection either. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Then the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the request from the Prosecution is granted in relation to Witness 31, reasons to be found in the three-prong test, that is, the witness or family living in Kosovo or intending to return to Kosovo; second is that the testimony may antagonise persons; third, the unstable situation in Kosovo as agreed upon by the parties. Then before we start with Witness 31, the witness expected to be called next Monday, I do understand that there are objections against any protective measures that would be requested by the Prosecution. The Chamber would like to receive written submissions on that as soon as possible. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Would Friday be acceptable?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we can think it over over the weekend. Yes, if that -- Friday is good. Preferably not 9.00 p.m. at night, but -- even if that would be the case, it's not dramatic. Then, Mr. Di Fazio, are you ready to call your next witness? MR. DI FAZIO: I am. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think the curtains should be down, because the protective measures are pseudonym, face, and voice distortion. Everything has been prepared for it. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: As she comes in, could I ask you to provide her with some assistance with taking the oath. Her reading is not good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness is not able to read. Then I'll assist the witness by asking her to repeat my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I simply record some anxiety about today's timetable, in the sense that if we are to get through this witness in chief and in cross-examination and the next witness, we will have to move at a truly cracking pace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Because there is a fair amount of ground to cover with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I am aware of that. And you may have noticed that I started in rather -- at a rather high speed. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm aware of that too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: And I'm going to try and deal with this witness as swiftly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: By way of assistance and getting matters moving, the first thing I'll want to show the witness, notwithstanding what I just said to Your Honours, just so that we can get through it quickly, is the pseudonym sheet. And I'll -- I'll tell her what the details are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: And that's going to be 65 ter 2088.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If Mr. Registrar -- MR. DI FAZIO: If we can get that ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the pseudonym sheet would accept what exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be P1108.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it already in anticipation the witness confirming that these are her personal details, that there's no objection against admission into evidence of the pseudonym sheet. Then we could immediately move to that. I see no negative responses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hoepfel reminds me that we should stay in private session for that moment -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because if the witness can't read, it's still to be seen whether she can read her own name. Sometimes people are able to do so. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. And also, some family details that I'll be eliciting as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon. Good afternoon. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Albanian spoken] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I can't hear -- the interpreters didn't hear what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please speak a bit closer to this microphone. Can you hear me in a language you understand? Witness 31, because that's how we are going to call you -- Witness 31, before you give evidence in this court, you -- the Rules require you to make a solemn declaration. Since I do understand that you do not read, I invite you to repeat the words I am now pronouncing. I solemnly declare. Would you repeat those words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know if the microphone as such -- is it switched on? Yes. Then please be seated so that's easier to be heard. If you sit down. And I don't think that there's any formal rule which requires a witness to stand when making a solemn declaration. So I would like to invite you to repeat the words, the words I am now pronouncing: I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand what they're saying. I do not understand what they are saying. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the witness on the right channel? MR. DI FAZIO: That's a question. It's got to be B/C/S. It's got to be the B/C/S channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: B/C/S channel.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters from the English booth interpreting normally from the B/C/S note that the witness speaks Albanian, not B/C/S at the moment. MR. DI FAZIO: She -- she speaks both. Yesterday when I spoke to her there was some confusion about the language, and -- and Mr. Smith, our case manager, notified all the parties concerned that she will testify in B/C/S. She speaks both, but B/C/S is preferred --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I first ask you whether you would prefer to speak the Bosnian/Serbian/Croatian language or whether you would prefer to speak Albanian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serbian is fine too, although my grammar isn't that good. As I said, I come from Yugoslavia and I do wish to speak Yugoslavian, but don't ask for me to speak the language gramatically correct. I can speak both Serbian and Albanian, but don't hold me to any grammar rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or perhaps German.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you'd prefer Albanian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's fine too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I invite you to repeat the words I pronounce and let's see whether the witness is on the Albanian channel. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the following words: I solemnly declare. Could you repeat those words: I solemnly declare. Then I suggest that we -- MR. DI FAZIO: Can I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We go to the language -- yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: I might be able to shed some light on this, if I can. Yesterday the witness came and saw me, and I thought that she was going to be speaking Albanian, and I arranged for an extremely competent Albanian speaker from Albania to interpret. Immediately, it became apparent to me that it -- the -- and the interpreter that she wasn't understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll move to the other language. MR. DI FAZIO: Then we switched to B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: And I spoke to her for about an hour or so in -- in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. MR. DI FAZIO: So I'm pretty convinced that that's the language that she -- she knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll then move to B/C/S. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: On an entirely different topic. If we could have the proofing notes, we'd appreciate them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: I didn't speak to her about the substance of her evidence. I spoke to her about the proceedings and what -- what would happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we now move to another interpretation. Do you now hear me in a language you understand, that is, Serbian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I invite you to make a solemn declaration, and I'll speak the words first and I invite you to repeat them. I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I would like to -- that you repeat those words, not to confirm that you understood them but you repeat the words I speak, that is, I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, my God. I don't understand well and I really don't see why. The lady who spoke to me yesterday, I understood everything she was saying. I can't understand what you're saying, or else if German could be speaken -- spoken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [German spoken] Ich koennte auch Deutsch sprechen und -- [In English] but that is not one of the official languages of this Tribunal. So therefore we have to speak -- we have to speak English. And I'm still trying to -- Madam Usher, the witness is now on B/C/S channel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I understand, but not that well. I don't understand fully what is being said, though. Not that well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will speak a few words in German to the witness, which might resolve the matter to some extent, and then we'll see from the questions and answers whether the communication is at a level good enough to receive the testimony of this witness. Madam Usher, I don't know whether the witness could also hear directly my words when I speak German. [In German] Zeugin 31, ich wuerde jetzt mal kurz Deutsch sprechen. Wir werden versuchen die Uebersetzung perfekt zu machen, aber im Anfang Ihrer Zeugenaussage ist es notwendig, dass Sie eine eidesstattliche Versicherung geben, dass Sie die Wahrheit, nur die Wahrheit und nichts als die Wahrheit sagen werden. Ich werde die Woerter im Serbischen -- ins Serbische uebersetzt, erst vorsagen, und dann sind Sie eingeladen die Woerter zu wiederholen, damit Sie selbst diese Erklaerung abgegeben haben. Ist das klar? Also ich wuerde jetzt fragen ob Sie Ihre Kopfhoerer wieder aufsetzen werden und damit Sie dann die Woerter, die ich spreche, die uebersetzt werden, dass Sie die wiederholen, damit Sie diese Erklaerung abgegeben haben. Ist das klar? Also, bitte. [In English] I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In German] Ja. Ich muesste die Wahrheit sagen. Ich schwoere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the words as they are translated to you, because German is not an official language of this Tribunal, so therefore --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Try to listen carefully to the interpreters and repeat the words, the words I speak, they translate to you, and you are then supposed to repeat. Yes? I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will tell you everything I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, would you please repeat literally the words, that is, "I solemnly declare."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will tell you everything. I don't know what else to tell you. I have no idea. Whatever I know, I will tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is that what you solemnly declare to us, that you will speak the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And will you tell us the whole truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And will you tell us nothing else but the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will not, by my life, I swear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has deliberated and considers that a solemn declaration has been given. If any of the parties would disagree, the Chamber would like to know it now, rather than at any later stage. MR. DI FAZIO: No. No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we turn into private session. But I first explain to you, Witness 31, we're not going to use your name. Your face cannot be seen by the outside world. And your voice is distorted as well, which means that although people can hear the content of your testimony, they can't hear your own voice as we hear it. Witness 31, you will first be examined by Mr. Di Fazio. Mr. Di Fazio, please proceed. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber if these things are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are we in private session? One second, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back into open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Witness, I've asked you now about those three boys. I'm just going to call them "those boys" from now on. We don't need to mention their names. All right? And I want to ask you about questions of things that happened in May of 1998. When did you last see those boys, those three boys?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/31
utterances.text: Ever since that day when they went missing, when they disappeared, we have not known anything about their fate. That was in 1999 or 1998. I'm not sure which year was that, but I was 16 years old at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And can you remember the month of the year? And if you can't remember, say so. But if you can remember the month of the year you last saw them, please tell the Judges.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/31
utterances.text: I do not know. I haven't done much schooling, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That's okay. Now, I'd like you to think back about the time when you last saw them, about the time you last saw them. Firstly, was it -- what time of the day was it that you last saw those boys? Was it in the afternoon or in the evening or in the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/31
utterances.text: It was around 10.00 in the morning that he went away, and nobody saw him again. I never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Well, just slow down. You -- did you -- on this occasion about 10.00 in the morning that you're starting to tell us about, did you see all of the boys together or just one or two of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/31
utterances.text: No, there were the three of them. They were on a horse-drawn cart.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know where they were going?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/31
utterances.text: Yes. They were going to Grabanica to have the corn milled for corn flour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And did they have grain on -- with them on the horse-drawn cart?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/31
utterances.text: Yes. They had a sack full of corn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was there a mill in Grabanica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/31
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Had you ever been to that place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/31
utterances.text: Yes. I used to go there before, because our mosque is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And do you -- do you know -- and again, I -- I ask you, make sure you tell us if you don't know something. Feel free to tell us if you don't know something. But if you know - if you know - do you -- can you tell us who owned this mill in -- in -- in Grabanica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/31
utterances.text: I don't know what his name is, but when we used to go there to mill the grain, we would see him there. I don't know what his first or last name is, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us if the man who owned the mill was an Albanian or perhaps a Roma or a Serb? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/31
utterances.text: He was an Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, you told us that the last day you saw these boys, they were on this horse-drawn cart on their way off to Grabanica. Did you ever see them again after they left to go to Grabanica on the horse-drawn cart?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/31
utterances.text: We didn't see them again. From that day, they never returned home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, are you aware if attempts were made to try and find them, to try and locate them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/31
utterances.text: Yes. I went with (redacted) to find them. Not at 10.00 or 11.00 but in the evening, when she returned from Pec or Djakovica. I don't know where she had gone. Because his mother was the breadwinner in his household.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And is that on the same day that you saw them leaving your village on the cart?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/31
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, just tell the Trial Chamber, please, slowly and go through it in -- in order, tell the Trial Chamber what you and (redacted) did to try and find these three boys.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/31
utterances.text: When she returned from Pec or Djakovica - I don't know where she was on that day - she came home and her husband told her that her son had not returned. She asked where he had gone, and she was told that he had gone to Grabovica to mill the corn. Next she took me with her to Klina. When we arrived in Klina, we searched for them there but we didn't find them. Then we went to Grabanica by bus --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can I ask you to stop -- just stop there. Just stop there. There's just one more detail that I'd like you to tell -- to tell the Court before you continue with your story. Could you just tell the Trial Chamber why you went to Klina if these boys had gone to Grabanica. Do you have any idea about why you went to Klina to look for them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/31
utterances.text: Because he had a -- a girlfriend there. His girlfriend was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Anyway, did you -- did you have any success or result or get any information by going to Klina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/31
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And then you -- continue your story. You told us that from Klina you caught a bus to -- to Grabanica. Tell us how that worked out. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/31
utterances.text: When we arrived there, (redacted) wasn't able to go on foot, because she had been begging the whole day. So when we reached Grabanica by bus, then we continued on foot. There was a forest on both sides of the road. We wanted to go through this quickly, and I went ahead of (redacted). There were some people who came out of the forest and stopped in front of me on the road and asked me where I was heading. I explained to them that (redacted) had gone to mill the corn but had not returned. The man told me that I could not proceed on the road. He grabbed hold of me and he wanted to rape me. But you see, I had a boyfriend before. When we were 12 or 13, we were tending to the cows and we -- he became my boyfriend. He showed up and he saved me. However, there was this other one who wanted to tear my clothes, rip my clothes off, but at that moment this boyfriend -- former boyfriend of mine appeared out of the forest and said, "Let her be. Leave her alone." I explained to them then that I was looking for (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/31
utterances.text: He let me past.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I just want to get a few more details. What I'd like to know a bit more is about these -- these people who -- who stopped you. You -- you said that there was -- first of all, when you were first stopped, when you were first stopped, how many people were there apart from you and your relative? About how many people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/31
utterances.text: The first time, only one person came out of the forest. Then all of them came out. Perhaps 100 of them. I don't know how many of them there were. But they all came out of the forest together.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Now, first of all, were they men or men and women or just men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/31
utterances.text: Only men.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did they have guns?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/31
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were they uniformed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/31
utterances.text: Yes. KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Continue your narrative, please, and -- and continue telling the Judges what -- what happened. You've told us so far that you were going in towards the town, that you were stopped, that you had a disturbance with one of the men, and that amongst the people there you recognised a boyfriend. Now, tell us how things developed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/31
utterances.text: I proceeded to the mill. I rang the bell there, and nobody showed up. I've forgot this bit, because it was nine or ten years ago. I had not yet set out to return when (redacted) showed up, and finally the man came out of the mill. (redacted) asked him, "My son was here today to mill the corn. Did you see him?" He answered, "No, I didn't see him at all." Next we returned, and on our way back we did not encounter anyone on the road. We returned home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. And did you get any news about the horse and cart at any later -- later time or about the boys?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/31
utterances.text: No. (redacted) mother, father, (redacted) uncle, (redacted) sister, and (redacted) sister’s husband, all of them went to the police in Klina, where they reported that the children had not returned. The police didn't know what to do. They told them to go back home. They returned home and the -- on the following morning they went to Klina. This is what I heard from (redacted) father, mother, sister, and brother-in-law, as well as from (redacted) aunt and uncle. This was something I heard from them. I did not see or observe any of this. Still I heard from (redacted) family that they had gone to Klina to the police there or -- I don't know. Perhaps even to the marketplace there. As they returned, there were two children there. I don't know whether they were Albanians, Roma, or Serbs. At any rate, there were two children who were running alongside a horse. (redacted) sister, (redacted) mother, and (redacted) uncle stopped the children, took the horse, and brought it home. When they brought the horse home, the corn sack was still on the cart but they weren't anywhere to be seen. And the horse was in good condition. And that's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for telling us that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Sorry. Was this your horse or the horse which had been taken from the boys?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That was (redacted) horse. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Same horse, same cart that you'd seen them leaving on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/31
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And I've just got one last question for you. You've told us about these three boys, and I don't want to use their names. Okay? So don't let's use their names. Now, you've told us about the Serb --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/31
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: On reflection, one of the boys you've told us was your -- was a (redacted). Did -- did he have any jewellery on -- on the day that you last saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/31
utterances.text: You mean what he was wearing or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yeah. On the day that he was -- that you last saw him when he went off on the cart, when the three boys went off on the cart, do you know if (redacted) had any ornaments on him? If you don't know, that's okay. But if you remember, tell us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/31
utterances.text: Yes, I know. He had a bracelet on his left or right hand. I'm not sure. And on that bracelet there was -- the name "Suzana" was inscribed, because this bracelet was given to him by his girlfriend. He also had his identity card on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you know Suzana?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/31
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What ethnicity was she?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/31
utterances.text: She was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you very much for answering my questions. MR. DI FAZIO: Oh, if Your Honours please, I -- I would ask that the pseudonym sheet be placed under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we should have -- I should have been aware of that. Mr. Registrar, pseudonym sheet to be submitted but still under seal. Mr. Emmerson. Witness 31, you have --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very -- very little indeed. I wonder if we might just go very briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we will. Nevertheless, I'll explain to the witness that she'll now be cross-examined by --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In fact, I'm going to ask that she remove her headphones for just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you take off your earphones for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Guy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When you were discussing your evidence with Mr. Di Fazio, you said - this is at page 17 - "I proceeded to the mill. I rang the bell there and nobody showed up. I've forgot this bit." And my question to you is: When did you remember this information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/31
utterances.text: I was afraid to ring. Therefore, I only pressed the ring once and I wanted to flee.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I understand. My question is: When did you remember this piece of information? Because you said "I forgot this bit." Did you remember that just as you were sitting here in court today? Or did you discuss this --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/31
utterances.text: No, I remembered it overnight. It's all coming back, the things I had forgotten. These things took place a decade ago. I had forgotten them, but now they're coming back. And (redacted) is someone that I dream of every night. I go to the mosque, to the church, but all is in vain. I cannot forget him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you very much. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Just one thing I think I ought to inform you of. It occurred to me just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session. That's fine, as far as you are concerned? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Please proceed. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Earlier today, before -- before this session started, Mr. Guy-Smith asked me about the proofing. And I said there had been none. And that's, in fact, correct. But there was a read-back to -- to the witness. And I don't know if that affects matters or whether that's going to change anything that -- that Mr. -- for Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Certainly not at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But I -- I would appreciate - and I believe that all Defence teams would appreciate - being informed before we'd proceed with the testimony of any witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- what precisely has occurred prior to their testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This is a repeated problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll move on at this moment, because for the witness it would not be good to have any further debate on that. Mr. Harvey, any questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I have no questions for the witness at this stage. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Mr. Di Fazio, I take it that there are no further questions to the witness? Then I would ask whether the parties would agree that the usual words I speak to a witness when the witness leaves, that I speak them in German, even if there would be no proper translation. I think that would accommodate the witness. I will add also one or two words, as I sometimes do, that the Chamber is aware that it was not easy to answer those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That would be fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: -- [German spoken] verstanden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. [In German] Zeugin 31, die Fragen sind jetzt alle gestellt worden, Sie haben die Fragen beantwortet. Ich moechte -- Sie koennen -- ich weiss nicht, ob Sie mich hoeren jetzt oder nicht. Ich moechte mich herzlich bedanken, dass Sie den weiten Weg nach Den Haag herkommen sind und dass Sie alle Fragen beantwortet haben. Und natuerlich haben wir gesehen, dass es fuer Sie nicht leicht war, die ganze Geschichte wieder in Ihre Erinnerung zu bringen, um darueber zu sprechen. Also, recht herzlichen Dank, und ich hoffe dass Sie eine gute Heimreise haben. Dankeschoen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [German spoken]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [In German] Dann werden Sie jetzt aus dem Gerichtsaal geleitet von Frau Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I know another witness is coming in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just because the issue is fresh in my mind. For some period of time we received no proofing notes with regard to any witnesses that have been presented. I am quite discomforted by the remarks just made by Mr. Di Fazio. We had offered a solution months ago with regard to a way of memorialising whatever you wish to call the meetings between the Prosecution and prospective witnesses right before they come to testify. I am troubled by what I've just heard. I remain troubled by it. I consider that at some point in time there has been some form of proofing or dialogue between prospective witnesses and the Prosecution prior to the witnesses testifying here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- with regard to information that we know nothing about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I at this point interpose my strong objection to this continuing practice and would ask for the Chamber once again to consider the notion of having these matters memorialised in some fashion either by tape recording or by video recording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I take it that other counsel join this objection or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think the Trial Chamber is -- is aware of the position that we've taken in relation to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- proofing sessions up until now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then the Chamber understands the words spoken by Mr. Guy-Smith to reflect the -- the thoughts of all Defence counsel. Is there at this moment a response to that? Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, there is. I repeat that there was no proofing. The witness -- I informed the witness of the general practices and procedures and what she's going to expect in court and who's going to question her and how it's -- how she's going to be questioned and the sequence of questioning. I gave her some insight into what the inside of this room would look like. I asked her about her journey and I asked her about her comforts at the hotel, and so on, matters like that. I then asked the interpreter who was present to read back the statement which was taken in English to her. She did. And that was the end of the -- the matter. I didn't ask her about anything in the -- in the -- in the -- any substance of the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the definition of "proofing" is -- if we look at the case law both of this Tribunal and of the International Criminal Court, then we'll be aware that the definition of"proofing" is -- that it covers a lot of things. And I would say that not under all definitions this would be not part of proofing. I don't think that at this moment we should have a further debate on it. But if you would revise -- if you would review the definitions given to proofing, then certainly reading back a statement might well be considered to be proofing. Now, perhaps the best way of dealing with the matter is that a transparent information to the other party would avoid, perhaps even if there was nothing, than to say, We met the witness. We just described the inside of the courtroom, and what the Judges looked like, different from parties, or that you -- that her statement was read back again to the witness. That would perhaps avoid objections as we heard them today. Avoiding is better than to -- to heal. Yes, that's the word. Are you ready to call your next witness? I see Mr. Dutertre coming into the courtroom. The screens will be removed. Mr. Dutertre, are you ready to recall Professor Aleksandric?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May then Professor Aleksandric be escorted into the courtroom. Would the parties agree that it would be sufficient to remind Professor Aleksandric of the solemn declaration he had given before, rather than to ask him to repeat it? I see no objections. Then we'll proceed in that manner. Awaiting the arrival of Professor Aleksandric, I do understand that although the parties were not in full agreement, that they compromised on the 92 ter statement, also in view of the testimony in chief given by Professor Aleksandric earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Professor Aleksandric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a while ago that you were in this courtroom. At the beginning of your testimony in this case, you gave a solemn declaration that you would speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. I would like to remind you that that solemn declaration still binds you in -- when continuing your testimony. Mr. Dutertre, you are aware that Mr. Emmerson has expressed some concern as far as time is concerned, so would you please try to reach the highest level of efficiency.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be, Your Honour, very briefly. I would like to ask to tender the 65 ter interview, which was signed by Professor Aleksandric and on which we have found a compromise. The text has not been fully drafted yet, and it has not been made available to you and not uploaded in e-court, but we have come to an agreement. The second point, I would like the index which was prepared this morning, sent this morning, and disclosed this morning to all the parties, as well as to the Bench, I'd like this to -- also to be tendered into evidence. And with this in mind, I would like all the exhibits mentioned in this index which have not yet been admitted as exhibits -- it's a -- this includes a small number. I would like these exhibits -- I would like these documents also to be tendered into evidence, and I would like these to receive an exhibit number. The Bench was informed of this this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As far as what you said, the 65 ter -- the statement, which is the 92 ter statement as well, I take it? It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It should be 92 ter. It shouldn't be 65 ter. It should be 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, has the witness already confirmed -- that's not my -- my recollection is not very clear on that, that he would give similar -- the same answers and that it fully reflects what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember that Mrs. Issa on your initiative had put the question to the witness. I don't have the transcript before me, but I believe that that is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Then is there any objection against the 92 ter statement to be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Certainly not in principle. We haven't yet had an opportunity to check the redactions that were agreed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- in the final version, but certainly not in principle. The Trial Chamber will have seen that have the Prosecution has filed a corrigendum correcting a number of typographical --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- and similar errors and certainly --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was about to talk about it. To ask for the admission of the corrigendum right now and to do this separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, perhaps, we invite Mr. Dutertre to make the whole list and then you respond to the ... So we have now 92 ter statement, the index, and the documents covered by the index. Yes. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The documents set up out of the index. We have the corrigendum, which I'm about to submit, and the report provided by Mr. Aleksandric on the report of Mrs --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's -- those are five documents all in all. Professor Lecomte's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The -- the comment by Professor Aleksandric on the Lecomte report. Yes. That's clear. Five documents. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I've certainly no objection. So far as the corrigendum is concerned and as I began to indicate a moment ago, it contains essentially a correction of a series of typographical errors. And without objecting or complaining about it or indeed making any point about it, I would simply observe that the -- in a number of respects these were the sorts of errors that Mr. Dutertre took Professor Lecomte to task for in the first of two schedules that he provided in relation to Professor Lecomte. But I certainly shan't be taking any objections to what are essentially typographical errors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, no objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No objections. No further comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey -- I don't see Mr. Harvey any more. Mr. Troop?

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you'll allow me, I'll call up the corrigendum, which is 2086, which is a 65 ter document. I would like the witness to authenticate this document. The usher has handed him a binder with all the relevant documents. The 65 ter number of this document on our list is 2086.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You put the relevant questions in relation to it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Professor, you now have this document on the screen before you. Do you remember having recently signed a corrigendum after the interview you had and would you make the same comments and provide the same answers as those contained in this corrigendum if these same matters were to be addressed orally today?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd therefore like to tender this into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the corrigendum will be P1109.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then finally, the comments on the report. --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I'd like to call up number 2089, which is a 65 ter document, on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Professor Aleksandric, what you see on your screen, are those the comments you made after reading Professor Lecomte's report and is that your signature on page 3? If we can turn to page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'd like to tender this document into evidence before putting questions about the report to the witness, so that is out of the way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1110, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. So we have now five documents or a series of documents on which we'll have to decide, that is, the 92 ter statement; that is, the index of the annexes to the report; and the documents -- the index and the documents covered by that index. Has that received a number already? Yes, it has. Then we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some of them, but not all. For the main part, they all have an exhibit number, but they don't all have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And how would we resolve that, to invite Mr. Registrar at this moment to assign numbers or have that done perhaps at a later stage? If there are no objections, I think we could deal with the administrative aspect of it at a later stage. Then we have the corrigendum and we have the -- the comments by Professor Aleksandric, that is, the last two being 1109 and 1110. In the absence of any objections, all these documents are admitted into evidence, precise numbers and listings to be completed as soon as possible. Mr. Dutertre, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will now address this issue on the merits.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Professor, I'd like to ask you whether you agree on reading this report with Professor Lecomte about the fact that the state of decay of the bodies depends on the -- on the environment and, more precisely, on temperature levels and humidity levels. And you are surprised that Professor Lecomte does refer to these climactic conditions that prevailed on the 13th of September. In addition, you are surprised by the fact that Professor Lecomte only refers to those climatic conditions that prevailed on the 13th of September. 13th of September. Page 22. In addition, you state that Professor Lecomte did not take into consideration bullet marks above on the wall below which the bodies were found, and in general terms you state that as far as the time those bodies spent on those locations, you could agree that if we were talking about a short period of time, if "a short period of time" means a few weeks, you could agree; but you wouldn't agree if "a short period of time" means a few days. And you say why you believe this is the case. Let me start off with an important point, which is the presence of bullet marks on the walls. You were there, Professor, you were on the scene at Lake Radonjic and therefore you were able to see these locations in situ for a number of days and the -- you indicated that there were bullet marks on the bones of the victims and bullet marks on the walls below which the bodies were found. So this is my first question: Why do you believe that these were bullet marks on the walls below which you found the bodies? Why do you say that these were bullet marks?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are bullet marks for the simple reason that it is precisely the type of traces left by bullets, by such type projectiles against a firm concrete surface.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And you have already seen those kind of bullet marks before in your career?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, many times during my career.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. This is my third question regarding this particular topic: What conclusion do you draw from the presence of these bullet marks on the walls below which the bodies were found? I would like to specify my question as to providing reasons for which these people died.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we carried out the autopsies and made the records, we established that it is impossible to ascertain the cause of death based on autopsy alone. However, if you are asking me for my expertise and since the autopsies established that there were injuries on the bones caused by projectiles and, on the other hand, we also have the fact of where the bodies were found, and literally just above them we found numerous bullet traces on the wall; all that, based on my knowledge and career, tells me that many of those people were killed at that very spot because of the bullets fired from a light weapon. I don't want to repeat myself, but you have it in writing as to what those bodies were exactly and which bullet marks were found. Next to that part of the wall, most of the bodies contained such bullet marks, and one can be -- one can conclude that many people were liquidated right there. I cannot be specific as to their names, and since I know them as numbers; therefore, I cannot tell you precisely which person was killed there, although there is a possibility that some of them had been killed on -- at a different location from a firearm and then brought there. However, the overall picture points to the fact that most or many of those people were actually killed on the spot by light weapons bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. I shall move on to another topic now, which is how much time these bodies spent on the scene. You were there, Professor. You spent a number of days there, a repeater, and you had a close knowledge and understanding of these bodies, and you say, in the last paragraph on page 2 of the translation in English of your report - let me quote - you: "[In English] On the video footage of a site, it can be clearly seen that almost all the bodies from near the cement wall -- found near the cement wall of the canal -- of the canal were in anatomical harmony; all parts attached. And due to the fact that they were in a severe state of decay and covered in soil, while they were placed in the body-bags, parts were literally torn off the face, so after we would remove the majority of the body, we would -- we would dig with our hands in the soil to try to find any missing bones." [Interpretation] Have I understood you well? I would like to make this clear to the Bench. Have I understood you well? Given the state of decay of the bodies in question and the state of decay was so bad that if the bodies had been placed there recently by the canal, you would have not found them in that condition; i.e., anatomical harmony, but parts of the body would have been dismembered? Have I understood you well?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In essence, you understood that well. To repeat, the bodies were in their anatomical set-up, as -- as a normal body would be, a head, a neck, a thorax, and so on. It is visible on the footage, because the camera moved as we were taking out the bodies. One can also see that as we were trying to recover the bodies, certain parts would simply detach themselves. However, when we found them, they were lying in a normal position, so to say, in an anatomical position. The bodies were not commingled or interspersed. Since we were placing those bodies in bags and we would not place those bags on any stretcher, since we had none, when the workers would pick up those bags, they would fold, they would bend, since they carried them by the -- the ends. The same happened when we were taking the bodies off the truck at the Pastrik Hotel and also when we transferred those bodies onto the autopsy table. Those are the reasons why the bodies and -- the bones and body parts were commingled. That was not because the bodies had been buried and then transported to the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I understand what you say by "commingled." In other words, it was the bodies belonging to the same body that were commingled. These were not bones from different bodies. Have I understood you well?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. When I say "commingled," I'm referring to the body parts of one and the same body. In my earlier evidence, I stated that we were trying as far as possible at the scene of the crime to establish which body parts belonged to which body and that was how we recovered them. Of course, since body parts were mingled with the soil, it was very difficult to establish right there and then which body parts belonged to which body. We, for instance, weren't able to establish with any certainty whether a certain body part belonged to person number 8 or not. We were able to establish that at a later stage as we were doing our autopsy, and then we established that there were body parts belonging to other persons as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Professor, I will get back to this at a later stage. Now, as far as body recovery is concerned and how things were, you talked about an advanced stage of decay and we realised that some bodies were covered in mud, R-11, R-12, because of the rain, and some bodies were -- like R-8, were covered by a lot of soil; R-13 and R-17 were buried. This is what we find in your 16th of September daily report, P412. Professor, what was the impact of the layout of these bodies in the mud on your ability to collect all the bones?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry. I don't understand the question. Maybe it's the interpretation. What was the layout?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I shall rephrase my question. How these bodies were placed. Were you able to collect all the bones of all the bodies that you found there; those that were buried or those that were covered in mud?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, most of the bodies were not covered by soil, because they were not below the ground. They were mingled with soil. In view of what the weather was like when we were there and what the prevailing weather conditions in that area were, most probably there were frequent -- there was frequent rainfall and there was a lot of mud. We could not conclude that the presence of mud meant that the bodies had been re-buried. It was the rain torrent that pushed the bodies. The second thing is that the bodies that you could see on the video clip are filmed just as we were working on them. You can see that some of the bodies were prone; others were lying sideways, and so on and so forth. But we were able to recover them as individual bodies, although, admittedly, with some bodies we weren't able to do that; like, for instance, with body number 8. We weren't able to do that at the scene. If I understand your question correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Will you allow for the possibility that for some bodies you were unable to recover on the ground and in the mud all the bones belonging to those bodies?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The video footage clearly shows how body parts detached from the body itself as we were trying to recover the body and put it into the body-bag. Of course, I do not rule out the possibility you saw on the video footage how we were poking in the mud with our gloved hands, admittedly, looking for the possible remaining bones, and therefore I cannot rule out the possibility that a bone may have remained in the mud here and there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that mud covered some of the bodies. I don't have it before me, but you also mentioned that there was soil on the clothing. According to you, the soil that was found on the clothing, did this soil -- was the soil carried by the rain?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, that must have been the soil indeed, because we did not notice any difference in the type of soil. For instance, when we were working at Batajnica, we were able to clearly distinguish between the local soil and the soil that had been brought over from elsewhere. As I was working at this scene, I did not observe any soil they -- that may have had different qualities from the local soil. That's why I didn't record it. Secondly, the clothing on all of the bodies was immersed in mud. It was stained with mud.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Was the mud the same as the mud surrounding the bodies? Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you've understood me correctly. I did not notice any difference in the quality of soil. The soil was clay, very sticky type of soil.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. Did you notice any traces of scavengers when you recovered the body? September 1998. Did you notice any traces of scavengers on the bodies in September of 1998 when you were by the canal?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One cannot notice this on the spot for the simple reason that the flesh and clothing were stained with mud. However, in the course of autopsies, you can see that we noted that some of the flesh was in a way riddled with some lacerations, lesions, which led us to conclude that this had been the result of scavengers who were in the area, and we noticed this as we were examining the bodies inch by inch. We could not engage in such an examination at the crime scene, because we had to recover the bodies and transport them first. Besides, you have to keep in mind the fact that we were working under war conditions. We were supposed to finish our job as soon as possible and leave this critical area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. You are establishing a distinction between what you noticed on the scene and what you were able to examine when you were back at the Hotel Pastrik. The presence of scavengers, could this explain the presence of some bones that belonged to certain bodies which you recovered in the canal?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Absence. Interpreter's correction: The absence of some bones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, scavengers or stray dogs or such-like creatures could have ripped off part of a body and take it elsewhere. I have to tell you that in the area we saw a lot of cattle herd straying around, a lot of stray dogs. And I'm telling you what I personally observed. In the area both on our way to attend the scene and on our way back, we were followed by stray dogs, entire packs of stray dogs running after us and barking.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. I just have two questions on this topic before moving on to something else. What is your opinion, Professor Aleksandric, on the conclusion drawn by Professor Lecomte? She establishes a connection between the absence of some of the bones, the presence of soil on the clothing, and the fact that the bones were intermingled -- and the fact that the bones were intermingled with the fact, on the other hand, that -- the fact that the bodies discovered by the wall had been tampered with or discovered elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I cannot rule out the possibility that some bodies may have been brought over from elsewhere, except for body 1, where -- which had bullet marks on it, but the two sacks on which the body was resting did not have traces of projectiles. I cannot rule out the possibility that some bodies were in fact brought over from elsewhere. But we have the possibility of various animals taking away bodies and, of course, we have the presence of mud. There's also the possibility that the bones were not initially commingled but, rather, that they became commingled as they were transported in the body-bag. I don't believe the bodies had been re-buried there, because I did not notice the presence of any other type of soil than the soil present there or, for instance, we did not come across a pine cone; whereas, there were no pinetrees in the general area. This is why there were no elements pointing to the fact that some of the bodies may have been killed somewhere else and then brought to that particular scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question on this topic: As far as you were concerned, the bodies had been there for a number of weeks. Have I understood you well?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I shall now move on to questions which are mentioned in Mrs. Lecomte's report, her observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not more than half an hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Half an hour was claimed, wasn't it? That would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... There where we express such concerns about time. Many, many questions the witness answers in the first or the second line and then he starts expanding on it, where you could easily stop him and said -- could thank him for having answered the question, and then he starts explaining other things which we might not be that much interested in at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall make it shorter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But -- Mr. Emmerson, how much time you'd think you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm certain that I can't shave my cross-examination down beneath an hour and a half, and that is already economising.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The neighbourhood of half an hour, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Half an hour. That makes altogether two. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: At this stage, I don't think I'm going to have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means that one and a half session at least would be needed by -- by Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, you have available 15 minutes after the break and I'll be --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... As usual. We'll have a break until ten minutes past 4.00 -- no, twenty -- quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There seems to have been some confusion. I think I said quarter past 4.00, but it is on the transcript twenty minutes past 4.00. Mr. Dutertre, you have time until 4.34. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: So first thing out of three, first thing, Mrs. Lecomte's report D266, page 18, 20, and 39 in the hard copy regarding the bodies, R-3, R-4, and R-13, there is no colonisation of the body by grass. I'd like to call up on the screen Exhibit number 418, page U016-4038. Page U016-4038. Could we please flip the page over and zoom in picture 81. If it could be on the -- 90 degrees to the left, please. Well, of course, we can look at it sideways. Bodies R-3, R-4, and R-13 are found down from the slope. On the picture, we see that down from the slope there is no grass. Professor, you told us that the ground was clay. So here is my question: Do you think it's normal or abnormal, curious or logical or surprising that there is no body found on these bodies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before the witness answers the question, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But perhaps we should first rotate the picture, which helps us to better see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I simply wouldn't want to let past a comment which does not seem to me to reflect what we see on the photograph. Plainly there is vegetation -- thicker vegetation higher up on the slope, but certainly it appears to my eye that there is vegetation along the base of the wall as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It depends which portion of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Exactly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Dutertre, if you are -- if you have in mind a certain portion of --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was thinking between where the -- cone 10 is and Professor Aleksandric, which is on the wall. So on this side, on this part of the slope, there is no grass.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I do understand that your question focuses on an area which appears left from the wall and which seems to be greyish in colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. As I understand it, Mr. Dutertre is speak about the area with the pile of gravel with the figure 10 on it and the figure in green who we understand to be Professor Aleksandric along the base of the wall. And whilst it may be well plain that the vegetation there is more sparse than it is higher up, to my eye there appears to be some considerable amount of vegetation along the ground --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the description -- Professor Aleksandric, if you just point at certain portions of the photograph without saying what you do see and what you do not see and I ask for logic, but first ask the witness to -- what he sees and -- and then perhaps come up with your follow-up questions. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I was going to make the precise injections regarding the photograph itself. In addition, raise the comment that with regard to issues concerning flora, there is no expertise that has been laid with regard to this witness, in terms of -- in terms of soil and vegetation growth. And since we are dealing with specific -- specifically one kind of flora -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll ask the question, 'cause I have a little time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, I do understand that you are --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Outside of the expertise again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Outside of the expertise of the witness. Let's see -- let's first hear the question, let's hear the answer, and then further explore what it's all about. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Defence was not challenging the fact that Mrs. Lecomte may have an opinion on this, because she's a forensic -- she's a forensic expert, as well as Professor Aleksandric.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: But, Professor, on the flat part, down on that slope -- along the wall on the left side of this wall, you were on site physically, so could you tell us whether there was grass growing at the bottom of the wall. And maybe the picture can help you answer this question.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person you can see back there is me. I was just younger by as many years. It doesn't strike me as surprising, the fact that there's no vegetation, because this is the slope which runs toward the wall but not only in that direction. There's a slope which descends parallel to the wall, and then we know that there was heavy waterfall, there were many torrents, probably not only just on the 13th, and the torrents caused the earth to move down the slope, and that's probably why we have the soil sediment there, as a result of the torrent carrying water -- carrying soil with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And between the pile of gravel and the place where you are, on that photograph, do you remember whether on the bottom of the slope, on the left, there was grass? What do you note and what do you remember?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really recall that after so many years. We can see that the vegetation is very sparse, though, and we can see that by the colour of the soil. But I want to stress something else. You see this pile of gravel on top of which there's the cone with number 10? This pile of gravel did not end up there as a result of the movement of the torrent. And the same applied to a pile of gravel further downstream, where body parts of bodies 14 and 15 were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Fine. Fine. Thank you. But let's focus on vegetation. You said that the vegetation was sparse. Do you believe that it was normal or abnormal, given the fact that that vegetation was so sparse, that no grass was found on the bodies R-3, R-4, and R-13, which were found at the bottom of that slope?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... In terms of it being normal or abnormal. The torrent brings earth with it. And the little grass that there was before that remains buried under that soil now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. I will move on -- I will move on to some -- to another topic, body R-5. Could we please have video -- video 452 to -- from 13.37 to 14.09. There's no dialogue on this video.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. You said body number 5?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Till 14.09? Could we play it again -- or continue, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And stop here. Professor, in her report Mrs. Lecomte said that R-5 is folded and placed on the ground. In the video which we just saw we see that above this body - this is body R-5. I think no one will challenge that - there is a surface where there is no vegetation. The grass was degraded. Maybe we can replay this. But I have a question for you. The fact that there is a decayed surface above body R-5, could this be explained by the fact that R-5 -- the body of R-5 would have slipped. It would have been buried in the first place in the place where the grass is decayed and then with time it would have slipped down for -- for reasons -- for reasons that we don't know of?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Same objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Same objection. And it also calls for a form of speculation well beyond -- well beyond this witness's expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We do not know yet. It depends on his answer. He could say "from my expertise," and if he explains, then -- let's hear his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You could as easily answer the question, Your Honour, as I could. This is not an matter for an expert opinion, in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's just as easy for you and me as for the witness, then, of course, you wonder why not -- but finally, if conclusions have to be drawn which are not within the specific expertise of the expert, then it could be for the Chamber to draw a conclusion sometimes on the basis of logic, on the basis of the interpretation of the -- of all the evidence considered in context. Let's hear the answer of the witness. Please proceed. Mr. Aleksandric, in a rather leading way it was suggested to you that the body might have been slipped from the place where the vegetation seems -- is -- at least, is not green and into that other position. Could you tell us anything from your expertise whether slipping in that direction could explain the situation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to remind you of the footage of the 13th of September, where you can see the torrent and the heavy rain. It is certain that it wasn't raining only on that day but before that as well. With such amount of rain, with such torrents, well, they simply take everything away, stones, soil, and it is not excluded that they can even move a body, a corpse, particularly a corpse significantly reduced in terms of its weight. It is putrefying or completely dried because of the sun during the preceding summer, and in that way the body was light. Of course, provided that the body had not been buried during that time. Body number 5 is on a slope in addition to all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. And may I -- may I draw the attention of the parties to it that from the answer of this witness, that at least we have now one new element, whether it explains everything, that is, that a body in a state of putrefaction is less heavy than under normal circumstances. I don't know whether it's -- will ever play any role, but that's at least within the expertise of the witness, I would say. Please proceed, Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: One last question - and this is not typos, because there were other errors in Mrs. Lecomte's reports - on the second report by Mrs. Lecomte, page 43 and 44, in the hard copy it's 41 and 43. It says there in this report that bodies R-14 and R-15 are found, on the surface of the ground for 14 and in the soil for 15 or laying on -- on the soil for 15. Now, in your own daily report, P412, page 3, this is your daily report signed on September 16, 1998, it mentions this, and I quote: [In English] "About two metres to the right of" --

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I interrupt you? I know by heart what it says, since I made the note. You can proceed with the question, and I can provide you with a comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so. We might not have it all, but we'll -- we'll find it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those are bodies 14 and 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P412, page --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What -- Professor, what do you think of Mrs. Lecomte's observations in that bodies R-14 and R-15 were found above the ground and, for R-15, it was flat on the soil?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I stated clearly in my daily report, we saw a lot of gravel, a pile of gravel rather than a body or parts of a body. Since we also saw some projectile damage on the pile, we thought that it might be some bodies inside; therefore, we cleared the gravel and we found bodies 14 and 15. It is not up to me to comment why the French experts concluded the way they did, but I believe that interpretation is incorrect and it was not the only incorrect one. Given time, I can go one incorrection at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think -- I'm not sure that Mr. Dutertre provided Professor Aleksandric with the transcript of Professor Lecomte's evidence in this regard, but the report refers to the bodies being, respectively, on top of -- of the ground --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had asked the question and --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... On top of the earth, and as you'll recall -- excuse me, as we'll recall, the testimony of the witness was that the bodies were above the surface of the ground, albeit that they were covered in rocks. In other words, in the interpretation of what she was describing was that the bodies were not interred beneath the earth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes that was -- I well remember that portion of the testimony. At the same time, what Mr.-- Mr. Dutertre asked what the witness recollection is of what he found assisted and what he wrote in his report and the interpretation of what was observed seems to be not the same by the French expert and the present expert. Please proceed, Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I add something? Although, rather, it does not tally with my opinion. It doesn't tally with what I saw and noted down. What I saw and noted down was a fact. I just found us another example. For example, for body number 10, the French expert said that there were no signs of the body being dried off. In the autopsy report, it is clearly stated that on certain parts the parts of skin were mummified and dry, dark in colour. As to why the French experts interpreted something incorrectly, as to why they interpreted something that was clearly stated in a document, well, it is not up to me to provide any comment on that. It is up to you, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, you earlier said this was the third and last question. Is that correctly understood? Time is over.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm done. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Professor Aleksandric, I want to start, if I may, just by understanding the parameters of the opinion that you have expressed about bodies R-1 to R-17 and, in particular, if we -- if we could just look at Exhibit P1110, that is, your most recent report. May I make it clear for the -- for the questions that I'm about to ask you at this stage, I'm interested only in understanding what you mean by your conclusions, not the reasons for it or the detail.
