But dealing specifically with the collection of remains that were recorded on the land side of the concrete wall, that is, R-1 to R-17, I just want to pick it up, if I may, in your -- in your October supplementary report, which in the original B/C/S is the paragraph beginning at the bottom of the first page, and in particular I want to ask you about the last few lines of that paragraph, which appear at the top of the second page. And in the English, it is the last five lines of the same paragraph, which also appear at the top of the second page. Now, can I -- can I see if I've understood the position correctly. As regards R-1, I think your view is that it can be concluded with relative certainty that that body was transported to the scene after death essentially because there was evidence of gunshot injury to the body but no evidence of projectile damage to the two bags which covered the body. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Although, I would omit the world -- the word "relatively." I would say "for certain."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as regards the remainder - so R-2 to R-17 - if we look at the last few lines of that paragraph, you say this, you refer to the projectile damage on the walls and you say: "First of all, having all this in mind, I think it can be concluded with high probability that many of the persons found had been killed from handguns on the spot where their bodies were found; whereas, it is certainly impossible to say it precisely for each individual, since the possibility that some of the persons found were brought to the place after death cannot be excluded." And you have supplemented that in your answers to Mr. Dutertre today - page 41, line 24 - where you fairly point out - and these are your words - "I cannot rule out the possibility that some of the bodies may have been brought over from elsewhere." Now, my question is in two parts: First of all, do you say -- is it your professional opinion that it is possible for you to say with certainty that any one of the individuals labeled R-1 to R-17 was killed on the spot where they were found, rather than being transported after death? And if so, can you please tell us which particular bodies you say can be identified as definitely having been killed on the spot?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, I can state that, since it is within my competence, all bodies that had projectile damage found on the scene, on one hand; on the other hand, the damage of projectiles on the concrete wall, these two things lead me to conclude, in addition to some other parameters, such as the bodies -- provided the bodies had not been buried previously and dug out, it all makes me conclude professionally that those bodies were killed there, they were liquidated there. Let's not use the word "liquidated." They sustained their injuries from bullets fired from hand-held weapons. Whereupon certain projectiles went through the wall, others missed -- through the body, others hit the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just stop there.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I conclude, please? I would like to conclude my thought. I haven't interrupted you before. Please do not interrupt me. Only for those bodies in which objectively it could not be ascertained in autopsy that they sustained any projectile damage, it is only those that I cannot say something for certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Emmerson is limited in his time. If f you have answered the core of his question where he earlier said that he was not seeking a lot of details, he is in a position to interrupt you. And, of course, I could allow you to finish your question if -- so therefore, that's one. Let me try to understand what you -- what you consider to be a conclusion. I would have no difficulties in understanding that if you see a lot of bullet marks and if you see bodies close to that which apparently also bear the impact of -- of bullets of -- of small weapons, then I would say that fits perfectly into a situation where the peoples were killed on the spot. At the same time, I also can imagine that the wall was used for training purposes and that the body was killed somewhere else by a similar weapon and then transported there. I mean, the conclusions, we have to carefully make a distinction between what is a conclusion which is a compelling conclusion or what is a conclusion which points at a likelihood of -- of lower or higher level. From what I understand from your answer is that, if you would know that someone was killed on the spot by a small weapon and where you find bullet marks both on the body and on the wall, that that would fit quite well in such a scenario, although such a scenario is not the only one you could think of under those circumstances. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely. That is why I cannot say things conclusively but most likely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So do we have the position clear? There were -- none of these bodies about which you feel able to say conclusively, they must have been killed on the spot?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, I cannot state that with absolute certainty. I can only say it is very likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. I'm going to put to you just, if I may, very briefly a passage of the testimony that you gave in the Milutinovic trial. And this -- if it's sought to be referred to, it's in the system as 1D53-0228 and I'm going to refer to page 5307 at line 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're going to tender that or not to tender that?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to read it into the record, so it's not necessary to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, the problem is then the Chamber is then also limited to the part you read.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's why I mentioned the reference. It is in fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But we have no direct access to that transcript at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, so it is available and can be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm just going to read to you a passage from the words that you used in the Milutinovic case about this scene generally. Your evidence there was as follows: "It is difficult to say whether all of the bodies we found at Radonjic Lake found their death there or elsewhere and then were transported and thrown into the canal. It is also questionable into which part of the canal they were thrown, because the water had carried them." And then a little later on, you referred to the pile of gravel under which bodies R-14 and -15 were found and the projectile damage on the wall and you said this: "So on the basis of the entire picture on the spot, on the basis of those circumstances and the post-mortems performed later, we could conclude that those two or three persons died there from gunfire and that they were later buried and covered with gravel." Professor Aleksandric, was that an accurate assessment that you gave to the Court in Milutinovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. However, I precisely stated that for the bodies that were in the canal, rather than those found next to the canal. On the other hand, I was quite precise concerning the bodies which, as you said, were not on the gravel but in the pile. On the site, we thought there were two people inside; however, during the autopsy of the bag number 10 we saw that there were some bodies which did not belong to that body. Therefore, we marked it -- those with 10.1. This is precisely what I have stated and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: When you were giving evidence in this court towards the end of your evidence in chief, at page 6819, line 13, Judge Orie asked you in terms about body R-1 in the bag and the evidence that you had given that that body had been moved and continued to ask you: Question: "Do you have any other indication for bodies to have been put there when not alive anymore?" And your response was: "No, I could say that definitely only for body number 1. As for the other bodies, I could only speculate." Now, the question I want to ask you is this: Is it really the position, Professor Aleksandric, that apart from body R-1, which you say conclusively had been moved onto the scene, the question of whether or not individuals died there or were brought there is, in your view, essentially a matter of speculation."

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, it is most likely that those people were killed by the projectiles there; however, that I cannot exclude the possibility that some bodies were brought there. Of course, it is up to the Chamber to decide what the case was in addition to all the other evidence they have before them.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Of course, and when I said at the outset I wanted to understand the parameters of your opinion. When you say it's possible that some -- some bodies were brought there, how many is some? As many as how many?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of numbers, it is hard to say. For example, in the case of bodies which did not sustain any projectile damage on the bones, however, they may have had damage through the soft tissue, such as the abdominal cavity, one cannot exclude that possibility. Therefore, to go into any figures, that would be a matter of speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Is it -- does it come to this, Professor Aleksandric, that you're saying that those bodies that had projectile damage you want to express the conclusion that they were likely to have been shot at the scene but those that didn't have projectile damage might have been moved there? Is that what your testimony comes to?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that as well. Although, I cannot exclude the possibility that somebody who had sustained damage -- projectile damage prior to being brought on the site was the case. I believe both can be plausible.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Exactly so. And finally on this question of general conclusions, I just want to put to you the opinion of Professor Dunjic on this question. This is transcript 7308, line 11. Question: "I'm asking you whether you would agree, Mr. Dunjic, leaving R-1 aside, that the other remains found by the side of the canal, as regards those remains, it is impossible to say with certainty whether they were moved there after death." To which the professor replied: "Yes, I could agree with such a statement that it is not possible to establish with certainty. But with a high degree of probability as a possibility, I would agree that those bodies were there. Now, whether they were brought there after death or were injured on the spot is something I cannot ascertain, that is, the site of death." Is that a conclusion with which you agree?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why are you asking me to interpret what others said? Ask me what I think. That is one thing. Another thing --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Think you agree?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes, because it is the same as mine. He said "with a degree of probability," as did I. And neither he nor me excluded the possibility of the bodies having been brought there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Emmerson, I just note that this -- already five minutes ago we were approximately at the same point. You're seeking to reconfirm that. I can imagine that for a jury that would be very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But analysis of probabilities and certainty, et cetera, et cetera, what -- whether the indicia fit into a certain scenario, whether there's an absence of any circumstance that would not fit in the scenario, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can tell you from my experience that my colleagues are rather sharp in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, to be sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I ask you now just about some of the language that you've used in your 92 ter statement. I don't call it up unless anybody wishes it to be put on the screen, but you have, I hope, a copy in front of you. At paragraph 257, you say this: "Bodies on the surface were likely present at that spot for a couple of weeks, but the bodies underneath the surface were probably there for a few weeks more than those found on the surface." And then at paragraph 259, you repeat in the last sentence that as regards the bodies on the surface, you would say that those bodies were at the location for a minimum period of a couple of weeks. Now, I just want to check a possible translation issue. In English, the expression "a couple of weeks" means more or less two weeks. "A couple" means two.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mean two weeks. When we say "a couple of weeks," it is equal to several weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So, again, can you give us a parameter? A minimum of what and a maximum of what?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What would be a minimum? Several weeks? Three or four? Plus/minus -- or rather, plus two to three weeks. It is difficult to say precisely because of the circumstances concerning which I agree with the French experts. There was often rain during the summer period alternating with high temperatures and the sun, and the rotting process after humidity is speeded up; therefore, it is difficult to say two or three weeks or in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could we call up, please, Defence document 1D66-0001. This is a -- a report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No number yet, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It has no number. I shan't been tendering it. I simply want to ask about one or two aspects of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I just ensure that we have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And could we, please, go to page 5 in the English translation, which I think is page 5 in the B/C/S as well. Whilst that's being brought up, Professor Aleksandric, this is a report on the autopsies and the examinations produced by Professor Dunjic in September 2001. And we can see that under this heading "Time of death" he analyses a number of factors that were taken into consideration and then sets out what he describes as the unanimous conclusion of the commission about the ages of the various corpses. And we can see in the first two lines of that table that for bodies R-1 to R-17 Professor Dunjic gives the earliest date of death as between three to five months. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Now, speaking as a layperson - and perhaps you can help me with this - if a body may have been dead for as much as five months but if, in your opinion, it could have been at the scene for as little as a few weeks, would you accept that the implication is that it may well have been somewhere else in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't exclude the possibility. I don't absolutely exclude it. But let me draw your attention to this: It says "commission" here. Which commission? Who signed that? I don't recall signing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, the evidence we've had is that the commission consisted of yourself and Professor Dunjic and other colleagues from Belgrade and that you formed yourselves into a commission at Hotel Pastrik for the purposes of certifying the post-mortems and conducting the identification of remains through traditional means. That is the commission I -- I understand him to be referring to.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we do something as part of the commission, then it is customary for all the members of the commission to sign what is made, and I don't recall signing this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not focus on this. First of all, the question was rather superfluous, I would say, because logic would give the answer without any doubt, and that's what the witness confirmed. And then let's not enter into a debate on matters which are not really at stake at this moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, just to focus on the paragraph -- the first full paragraph there, where Professor Dunjic indicates the factors that were taken into account in determining the date of death, autopsy findings, prominence of corpse characteristics, corpse changes, and so forth. And we see that amongst the criteria listed is the presence of larvae, worms, and insects. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And we can see and have seen in a number of the post-mortem reports that records are made of the presence of motile cylindrical maggots which are then measured and given a length. My question is, could you just explain in one sentence why as a pathologist you would consider that relevant to the estimation of death? Just in a sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a sentence. In and of itself, this cannot be relevant. It can only be relevant within all the other parts of the mosaic that were in fact referred to here by Professor Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I entirely understand that. It's a factor. But -- but it's been suggested in this court that unless you know the precise species and its life cycle, the presence of larvae should never even be recorded in a post-mortem report, because it is irrelevant. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree with that. When performing an autopsy, we are duty-bound to record everything that we find. If an explanation needs to be provided that goes beyond our expertise, then we coopt into our commission specialists in other fields, such as, for instance, biologists. Then we provide an opinion on behalf of the commission and everybody signs that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now -- we can leave that document now. In your assessments, Professor Aleksandric, obviously as we've seen and as you've explained, you attach considerable significance to the presence of projectile damage, that is, gunshot marks, on the outer canal wall near to the pile of gravel underneath which bodies R-14 and R-15 were found. And I want to ask you some questions about that. And for the purposes of these questions, I want you to imagine that you are looking towards Lake Radoniq. So when I refer to "the right wall," I am referring to the wall nearest to where the bodies were found. And when I refer to "the left wall," I am referring to the wall furthest away from where the bodies were found. And obviously the inside and outside of each wall is self-explanatory. Now, first of all, am I right in thinking that physical projectiles, that is, bullets, were recovered from some of the remains?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they were. I can't recall the details now, but it is all stated in the records.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And do you know whether any attempt was made to retrieve the projectiles, that is, the bullets lodged into the canal walls in order to make forensic comparisons?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wonder whether that's what you're thinking about as well, Mr. Dutertre. Where's the evidence that any bullets were lodged into the --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I can put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- that's what I've suggested. Was that your point --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My objection was that nothing says that there were bullets lodged into the wall. There -- there's traces of impact, but there are no bullets in the wall. So this is -- this question is based on speculation, which is why I raise this objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The witness was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, where I used three lines to say exactly the same, Mr. Dutertre, you repeated it again in five lines. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Professor Aleksandric, did you look at the projectile damage on the walls in detail?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I don't recall whether there were any projectiles lodged there. Based on my experience, one ought not to expect any bullets to remain lodged there, because that was firm concrete material. Besides, it is not down to us to examine bullets; it's down to the forensic specialists from the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm not -- I'm not criticising you. I'm just trying to understand whether, as far as you know, any lead was retrieved from the wall for any forensic comparison. And do I take it that your answer is that you're not aware of that occurring?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, here again two things are confused: Lodged into the wall and retrieved from the wall is not exactly the same. You can find bullets at the bottom of the wall and they can be collected, and that's, of course, not exactly the same. So you're moving from one specific issue to a rather general issue which --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- might easily confuse the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand. In relation to casings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'll put the question finally again just to make sure there's absolutely no misunderstanding about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: As far as you are aware, do you know one way or the other whether any lead bullet pellets were removed from the wall for a forensic comparison? Removed from the physical fabric of the wall.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's understand each other. A casing cannot be found in the wall, because a bullet consists of a charge and a casing. A bullet charge may hit the wall; whereas, the casing is ejected and drops normally on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I may interrupt. Mr. Emmerson's question was focusing on the bullet --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- itself. Not on the casing, not on anything else. Just the part that flies. Please proceed. Please answer the question by --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. That's how it was interpreted to me. Can I hear the question again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. The question is: As far as you are aware, was any attempt made to remove the lead -- any lead bullets that may have been lodged in the wall for forensic comparison with the lead bullets that were recovered during autopsy?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I don't know and I don't remember whether a bullet had been found in the wall. I don't recall one having been found on the ground either. Had I found a bullet by any of the bodies when I was recovering them, I would have placed it in a special bag and labeled it. I believe that a bullet case was found, but let me check this.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I ask you not to trouble on that, because we've heard other evidence in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll move on, Professor Aleksandric.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Apart from the projectile damage on the outer aspect of the right wall close to the pile of gravel, do I understand your testimony correctly - and of course, we've seen the video - that there was also projectile damage on the inside of the left wall, that is, the opposite wall?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I should look at the footage. On the outer aspect of the right wall, looking at the canal downstream, some piles of gravel were found, and this prompted us to search for bodies in the pile. Now, whether there was also damage to the inner aspect of the left wall, I can't recall all that after so many years. I would have to look at the relevant documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. What I want to focus on just for a moment with you is bullet damage going in the opposite direction; in other words, you're describing bullet damage which would have been inflicted from the right side to the right wall outer aspect. I want to explore with you bullet damage inflicted going in the opposite direction, to the outer aspect of the left wall. Now, the Trial Chamber has heard testimony already from a witness, Witness 64 - I won't mention his name - but he was the crime scene technician who accompanied your team and made a video of the operation. And he has testified - page 7862 - that having reviewed the videotape, he could confirm that there were bullet marks also on the outer aspect of the left wall, that is bullets being fired in the opposite direction which can be seen on the videotape; in other words, the area where no bodies were found. And I wonder if we could just play one -- just less than one minute of videotape which shows that. It's Exhibit P72, at time counter 13.43 to 14.30.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I remember that, and I don't need to watch the footage. But bodies were not found below. The damage to the outer aspect of the left wall were to be found toward the end of the concrete wall right before the plunge into the natural course of the canal.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. If you can just confirm for us, please, that that is the passage that we are looking at on the video now.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just bear with us until it concludes so that we can see exactly where we are. Thank you. Now, as you rightly point out, no bodies were found in that location. But -- but you were aware of those bullet marks at the time, were you?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Now, obviously nobody can know whether the bullet damage to the left-hand wall and the bullet damage to the right-hand wall occurred at the same time or at different times, but in the assessment that you've made here of relative probabilities, did you take account of the possibility that this could have been an exchange of fire across the canal between opposing forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I object to this question which is of a purely military nature. And I don't think Professor Aleksandric can answer this question, which are at any rate of a speculative nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think whether it was an exchange of fire -- but if -- if Professor Aleksandric draws conclusions from the presence of bullet marks, then other scenarios may be put to him to see whether they would in any way attack his conclusion. And it has got nothing -- it could be hunters as well. It has not a specific military character. Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The question was, Professor Dunjic [sic], whether in expressing the opinions that you have rather confidently expressed about some of this material, whether you took account of the possibility that the bullet marks you've seen on the outer aspects of the right wall might have been inflicted in the course of an exchange of fire across the canal, given that there were bullet marks on the outer aspect of the left wall and no bodies there.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the left wall, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, there are -- as we've seen, Professor Aleksandric, there are -- there's projectile damage to the outer aspect of both walls - in other words, bullets being fired in both opposing directions - and the question I'm asking you is whether in coming to your rather confidently expressed conclusions you took account of the possibility that there may in fact have been an exchange of fire between opposing forces across the canal.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having in mind the fact that the damage was to be found on the outer aspect of the left wall and that it was rather concentrated in a circle, I wouldn't say that this was the result of an exchange of fire, because the -- in that case, fire would normally be aimed at the area beyond the wall. I believe that this was the result of a body being shot at and then dumped into the natural course of the canal.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm just trying to explore how open-minded you were in these conclusions, Professor Aleksandric, because people when they're firing, as I'm sure you'll readily agree, sometimes don't always hit their target.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. But if in the middle of that wall - and when I say "in the middle," I mean the central part when looking at the wall from the bottom to the top - that's the opinion I gave you. You asked for my opinion. I am dealing with this matter in an entirely professional manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has heard evidence from a man called Zarko Bajcetic, who was a senior official of the RDB in Djakovica, who attended the canal scene on the very same day that you arrived, the 11th of September. And he has testified that from the beginning of July onwards there were a number of armed clashes between Serb forces and the KLA in this area and, specifically, that there were armed clashes between Serb forces and the KLA in the very place where the bodies were found by your team. That is transcript 6529. Can I ask you: Were you aware of that when you were making your evaluations?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was fighting everywhere, including the place where the bodies were found. I know from the stories that I heard upon our arrival there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So you were aware at the time that over a period of months there had been armed engagements in that very area where the bodies were found? Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to know what evidence there is to state that there were military engagements in this particular area. Could we be given a reference in support of this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I did give the reference --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson gave 6529.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The question in re-examination from Ms. Issa of Mr. Bajcetic in relation to the armed engagements he'd described goes as follows: Question: "Are you aware of whether or not any clashes took place in the specific area of where the bodies were ultimately found?" Answer: "There were clashes in that area as well." Now, you just told us, Mr. Aleksandric, that you knew that there was fighting in the place where the bodies were found and that you knew that from stories that you heard on your arrival. Just tell us a little bit more about that, please, if you will. When, as far as you understood it, had the fighting taken place in the area where the bodies were found?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. When I said "the area," I meant the broader area, including the place where the bodies were found. When there were clashes there involving -- I don't know whether it was the VJ and the MUP together, and when they drove the Siptar army out of the area, I only know that as a result of that fighting -- or after that fighting the bodies were found there. Now, where the individual participants to that fighting were exactly located, I don't know that. I only know that there was fighting going on and that after the area was liberated, bodies were recovered there. Now, if you're asking me whether there was an exchange of fire from two opposing parties across the canal, I don't know that. I don't even remember that we spoke about that specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. In your supplementary report, as Mr. Dutertre emphasised a little while ago, you -- you have indicated that in terms of the length of time that bodies may have been at the site, you're unable to accept Professor Lecomte's conclusion that they had been there for a short time if by that she means a few days, but you could accept it if it meant a few weeks. Now, she has testified that she does indeed mean a matter of days when she uses that expression and, indeed, that in her view it is more likely than not that these bodies had been moved. What I want to do is to try to explore the difference between you as to what you mean by "a short period" by reference to evidence that we have heard from a lay witness in this case. And for this purpose, I am referring to Witness 21 and to the evidence that he gave. First of all, can I ask you this, Professor Aleksandric: When you gave evidence in this case a little earlier in your evidence in chief - this is transcript 6737, line 24 - you told the Trial Chamber that when you arrived at the canal on the 11th, you immediately saw corpses lying on the ground adjacent to the canal wall. You said: "These were the bodies that we were able to see in that patch of grass." Can we assume therefore that when you first arrived, the bodies that were located on the surface that you were referring to in that answer were easily visible to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has heard evidence from a lay witness who -- who said that he visited this area, the precise area we're discussing, the end of the concrete section of the canal, on two consecutive days looking for missing relatives. He gave an estimate of about one and a half to two weeks before he attended Hotel Pastrik for the identification process on the 18th of September, which would put his visit at some point during the first week of that month. I see Mr. Dutertre has a point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dutertre. What -- what would you like to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just waiting for the end of the question. I was anticipating on an objection. But I will first wait for the end of the question before I raise my objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sometimes the witness's answers - and I don't always hear the end of the translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not blaming for your standing and waiting, which is very wise, I think, but I would like to hear your objection now. Or is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether Mr. Emmerson has finished putting his question. At any rate, I haven't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He has not put a question yet to the witness. He's just referred to testimony that the Chamber have heard and has summarised that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going, if I may, just to conclude and then put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So, if I can just recap. This is a lay witness who on his timing of events would have been in this area during the first week of the month. And he testified that he crossed the section of the canal where the semicircular section gives way to the concrete cascade across a wooden bridge, both ways, that is to say, on four occasions on two subsequent days. And he told us that on the second occasion he walked up as far as the Economic farm and came across a large number of bodies in various locations, including a number of bodies inside one of the cowsheds at the Economic farm. Now, you gave some testimony in your evidence in chief about having been inside one of the cowsheds. I think, from your daily report, it appears that you went inside both cowsheds when you were there on the 11th. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. We went into all the buildings. As far as I remember, there was one on the left-hand side and the other one on the right-hand side. And in one of those, we found the cables tied to horizontal bars.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But certainly there were no human remains in either of the cowsheds when you got there on the 11th of September, were there?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Had there been any, I would have written it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The same witness also testified that on both occasions when he crossed the canal he was able to see two bodies lying in the water in the concrete section of the canal. I don't trouble you about those two bodies, because we've seen some photographs in relation to those, but his evidence was that he had not seen any bodies lying on the ground in the area adjacent to the wall where you found R-1 to R-17. And my question is this: Do you accept, given this question of "a short time" and the difference of opinion between yourself and Professor Lecomte, do you accept that it is possible that those bodies were not on the surface there on the 1st of September?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Crossing over the bridge four times I don't think is particularly accurate, but that's not the main point. If we assume that the witness has not seen the bodies, that there were no bodies, I think there is something that is being suggested in the way in which Mr. Emmerson is putting his question, so obviously this is a problem and I object to this question. It's hugely speculative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, I was imagining how you could ever justify a -- an answer that would say, No, I exclude for that possibility if the witness has not been there at any earlier stage but --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It -- the issue here is a specific difference of opinion between himself and Professor Lecomte --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- as what is -- as what is to be meant by "a short time." Now, Professor Lecomte's testimony is that by "a short time" she means a matter of days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: This witness's testimony is that he means a matter of several weeks. And we have here testimony which, if true --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but at -- but at the same time, this witness testified that he cannot exclude for the possibility that the bodies were moved in there, so therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. But the question is: When?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But could -- well, let's move on. I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, put the question to the witness, because I won't know -- I don't know to what extent it would assist us in reaching any conclusions. But let the witness answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could -- Professor Aleksandric -- oh, I'm sorry, another objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just an observation I'd like to make. Witness Avramovic [phoen] commented a number of -- on a number of video clips. It depends where you are located. It depends where you are standing. Sometimes you see things. Sometimes you don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is rather comment than objection and it could have been in -- in re-examination it could have been raised. Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The question, Professor Aleksandric, is a reasonably simple one: Do you expect that it is possible that the bodies that were on the surface were not there on the 1st of September? And you say they must have been there for a short -- you accept that they could have been there for a short time, depending on how we define that. Would you accept that the 1st of September, that the -- that what you saw was consistent with the bodies having not been there on the 1st of September?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll be brief. No. I can explain everything I've said so far. In addition to the impression I gained on the spot, judging by the soil that was over the bodies brought there by the torrents - therefore, it was mixed with the bodies that were on the surface or immediately below the surface - such a thing cannot occur in a mere ten days' time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to turn, if I may, to the bodies in the water now for a moment, and you indicated a little earlier in answer to a question from me about your testimony in the Milutinovic case, that when you said there that it was difficult to say whether bodies had been transported and thrown into the canal after death and when you said it was questionable which part of the canal they had been thrown into because the water had carried them, that you were referring specifically to those bodies found in what we will call the natural section of the canal. Can I ask you this: I'm going to put some specific questions to you about a collection of bodies which were labeled R-21 to R-24 a little -- in a little while, if I may. Leaving those bodies aside, is it correct that all of the bodies from R-19 onwards, all of the human remains from R-19 onwards, are remains which, in your view, were likely to have been washed into the position in which they were found?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are talking about human remains. R-19 -- and in the daily reports of Professor Aleksandric, R-19 is in fact no more than clothing. So maybe Mr. Emmerson could clarify what he is asserting here before putting his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: First of all, I don't think Mr. Dutertre is correct. I think that it was the glove -- the epidermis, that is, of a human hand amongst R-19. But secondly, I'm simply asking the witness: Leaving R-18 out of account for a moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You just excluded R-21 and R-24?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm coming back to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From R-19.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that's another question now.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, from 19 upwards, which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 19 upwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Which is the remainder of the remains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So from R-19 upwards, whatever you find as bodily remains, R-21 and R-24 excluded from your consideration, and then the question would be, Mr. Emmerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I'm trying to do this shortly and compendiously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, we now first give an opportunity to Mr. Emmerson to --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't wish to get in anybody's way, but if we exclude R-21 and R-24, there is a connection and we did disclose genetic reports to the Defence teams and R-27, there is a connection with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Dutertre, let me be quite clear and that is as well for all parties. We are not here in a debating club. We are in the course of a cross-examination. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let's do it the long way round, if we may.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let me start, please, with R-20. R-20 you deal with in your witness statement at paragraph 167, and there you indicate in respect of that body, which was found trapped beneath a clay rock that, in your view, that was most probably carried there by the flow of water. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Now, one more attempt to do it compendiously. Leaving aside the collection of bodies R-21, R-22, R-23, and R-24, that collection that were found together. Leaving them aside for a moment, is it your view that from R-20 onwards we've just looked at, all of the other remains are likely to have been washed into the position in which they were found by the flow of the water?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can almost say that for certain, since I cannot recall the exact numbers, but let's say body 29 was mixed with some branches. It couldn't have happened had it not been for the torrent.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. So -- and we can find each of the other examples where similar points were made, but the -- but the general proposition is there clear. I wanted to ask you about one specific body in that connection, body R-32. Now, in the evidence that you gave in chief in relation to that body -- I'll just read, if I may, one answer. This is at transcript 6806. You -- you were asked by Ms. Issa to estimate how long the body had been in the water, and initially you said: "It must have been there for several weeks." And then she asked you -- this is 6806, line 20: "And can you be -- you are unable to be specific as to what you mean by 'several weeks.'" And you replied again: "At least four to five weeks. Perhaps a week less. We can't assert with any certainty that the body was in the water all the time. It may have been on dry land for some time and then two weeks prior to its recovery it was thrown into the water." Now, I just want to explore, if I may, briefly that hypothesis with you. When you said that from the appearance of R-32 it was a body that could have been on dry land for some time and then thrown into the water two weeks prior to its recovery, was that you expressing the view that it may have been dead on dry land?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a way, yes. But that doesn't necessarily mean that it was outside the canal. It was -- maybe it was in the dry part of the canal where there was no water and then the torrent came and picked it up. For example, such as body 29. It is carrying a Bordeaux shirt. However, I wasn't there on that day when the footage was made. I did see the footage, and you can see two bodies, one of which had a red or Bordeaux upper clothing item; therefore, it is very difficult to say whether they were completely out of the canal, dead for some time and then thrown in, or what time exactly they ended up in the water, whether it was at the time they were killed. They also could have been on the dry part of the canyon, such as the bodies 21, 23 -- what was it? 21, 22, 23, and 24, that group of bodies that was in the dry part of the canal. One cannot say anything precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I entirely understand.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, as regards body 32, there is photo documentation in existence. We established that the cranial roof was at the beginning of the earthen part of the canal. It was 18/1. In other words, one may conclude that that body ended up in the natural part of the canal. It was thrown in the canal at the very beginning of it. However, I cannot exclude the possibility that the body was at a certain point in the water part of the concrete part of the canal. I can only interpret what I saw. If the cranium roof is at the beginning of the earthen part and the body is further downstream, that part of the skull must have been remained there stuck in some branches perhaps and the torrent carried the rest of the body downstream until it got stuck somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. That -- and that, you're referring to R-18/1, which is a fragment of skull found close to the foot of the waterfall. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. That is the part of the skull, the cranial roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And R-32 had been washed right to the very end of the canyon.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean exactly by "washed"?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry. It had been carried by the water right to the very end of the canyon.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when something is carried by water, as you can see on the footage, you can see that there are twigs, rocks. The water can take a body up to a certain place. Then it gets stuck. After a few days, it continues its journey onwards. One cannot say where that body was at any given time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Can I then in that context just ask you about paragraph 247, briefly, in your 92 ter statement. You -- you refer there to some information that you received from the divers that were assisting you. And this is about halfway down paragraph 247: "The divers also told us something that I also read in Professor Dunjic's documents. They said that at the mouth of this river there is a large quantity of mud in that position and there were lots of branches, and this was an obstacle, and they concluded that it was impossible for any body to flow into the lake. So practically, we believed that this would be the last body that would be found." And you're there referring to R-35. Now, I want to understand this. We obviously have the divers' reports. We can look at them if we need to. I'm just looking at the --

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not necessary. I'm familiar with that, and I believe you have that document. It was the record made by the diving team. It is not only what we said that we were told by them. There is a report by the diving team specifying that. I suppose you have that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We do have it, and it does, as you rightly summarise, express the conclusion that it would be impossible for a body to be washed into the lake. I just wondered, in that context, if we could go back to paragraph 204 in your witness statement. Could we -- do you have that? 204. Professor Aleksandric, paragraph 204 in your witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksandric, can you find that? Paragraph 204.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The last sentence of that paragraph expresses the view that: "It is possible that some bodies were washed into the lake before we managed to collect them." I wondered if you would be able to assist us as to how you reconcile that with your acceptance in paragraph 247 of the advice that you were given by the MUP divers that it was impossible for bodies to be washed into the lake.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can reconcile that easily. We were not at the far end of the lake. We were in the initial third of the canal. From that perspective, we thought that some bodies may have been carried out to the lake. We were there on the 13th and the 14th when the torrent was strong. We thought that some bodies were washed into the lake. However, those who were on the site, the specialists, being the divers, concluded that it is impossible for the reasons they explained that some bodies ended up in the lake. The conclusion, therefore, is that all those bodies carried downstream by the torrent reached the end of the canal. I see nothing contradictory in that. It was our view from that spot at the beginning of the canal that those bodies may have ended up in the lake.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just so that we're clear, for the record, then, the last sentence of paragraph 204 reflects a view that you held in the interim but that you then abandoned when you got official advice from the divers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. We said it is possible. We did not assert that. And then the divers said it was impossible. There was no further discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I've just got one further topic before I ask for a short adjournment, a short break. I wonder if the witness could be given the yellow file for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And perhaps you could assist him by turning to tab 16C, which in the English is 16D, which if I may look for one moment, is D131.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I won't go through the details of this part of the divers' conclusions, but as you rightly say, they -- they draw the conclusion that we have just discussed. I simply wanted to ask you this: If you could look into the B/C/S version at the first paragraph on the second page. And in particular, at the last line of that paragraph, which in the English translation is the second paragraph on the second page. It refers there - this is the divers refer - to finding for them the first body on the 15th of September around 700 metres from the beginning of the canal. "The current had thrown this body underneath a rock. Following the discovery and marking of the scene, the investigations team, under the supervision of team leader forensics expert Dr. Branimir Aleksandric, the body was taken out of the water and taken away for forensic examining." And then it says this: "Found in the vicinity of this body was a coat probably belonging to the regular police uniform of a regular of -- of a Republic of Serbia MUP member." Now, we haven't found any evidence in your records of that police uniform or coat being recorded, and I wonder if you could just help us. First of all, do you know which body this is referring to? Are you able to tell?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the description stating that the -- the current -- just a moment, if I may -- where it is stated that the water pushed the body underneath the rock, I conclude that this was body R-20. I see that there is a difference in terms of metres. The police said 700 metres; we put in around 500. I don't think that is important, since no one measured that distance with a tape. But approximately in terms of the number of steps and the general impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And as for the police coat, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the police coat, it wasn't on the corpse and we did not believe it was part of the clothing of that body; however, we did state that it was found in the vicinity. As you can see from the daily reports I drafted, we registered all those items of clothing found along the canal that could not be associated with any particular body in situ was put in the bag number 34.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You have used from your one hour and a half until now one hour and 11 or 12 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm -- I'll finish well within time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well within time. Because if we could save some time so that Mr. Dutertre has at least an opportunity to -- I don't know how much time you would need to -- if the estimate would still be half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I -- no, as a matter of fact, I'm going to have a conversation with -- with Mr. Emmerson during the break and will be ceding some of my time to Mr. Emmerson based on the questions asked that cover areas that I was going to go into, and I don't see any reason to gild the lily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey, no changes in your estimate?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I might have a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You might have a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: A question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're looking forward to it. We'll have a break until ten minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just to indicate, we've consulted amongst ourselves and adjusted our times very slightly so that -- Mr. Guy-Smith has kindly indicated that a little of the time that he had set aside might be used to complete cross-examination which is relevant to more than one accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I want to turn now, Professor Aleksandric, to the group of remains R-21 to R-24, which is the one group that you suggest in your statement and in your evidence in chief you thought most likely at least one of that group had been thrown into the canal from above, rather than washed into the position in which it -- it or they were found. And, first of all, let me just summarise what I understand your evidence on this to be. Just to recall the position, R-21 and R-24 were respectively the upper and lower parts of what turned out to be the same body; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But at the time that you were conducting the recovery operation, although you thought that was a possibility, it was at that stage no more than a working hypothesis until the post-mortem was conducted; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, the hypothesis that you have explained in your statement and in your testimony in chief is that at least one of that group of bodies, R-21, R-22, R-23, and R-24, may have been thrown down from the top because you found two shoes which together were labeled "R-25" higher up in the vegetation in the area where that group of bodies was discovered. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And the two shoes were found roughly 3 metres apart from one another; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And the lower of the shoes - that is to say, the shoe nearest to the remains - was about 3 metres up the bank from where the remains were found; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And the shoes were found in an area which was vegetated - there was growth there - which led you to conclude that the level of the water could not have risen to the point where the shoes were found. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is due to the fact that in the area where the torrent washed through, you practically have no vegetation. And, of course, wherever the torrent passes, it washes everything before it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The bodies themselves were found lower down in an area where there was no vegetation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And your conclusion, so that we understand it, your conclusion is that because the shoes were found higher up and because one of the bodies in that group had no shoes, your hypothesis was that those shoes found higher up may have originally belonged to that body that was found without shoes. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In which case you would then conclude that it would imply that the body must have passed through the area where the shoes were found. Is that -- is that what it comes to?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. So, again, if I can just pause here. There were two steps, if I may put it this way, would you agree, in your reasoning: First, an assumption that the two shoes that were labeled "R-25" had belonged to the body that was R-21 and R-24; and secondly, an assumption that because R-21 and R-24 was found about 3 metres away from bodies R-22 and R-23, then all three might have reached the position where they were found in the same way. Is that a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I just want you to help us, if you can, to help us clarify some confusion, then, that arises in your 92 ter statement. Can we look at paragraph 177 first, please. So 177 of the 92 ter statement. Thank you. Now, in the second sentence of that paragraph, you say -- you say this: "We believed that the shoe found higher up belonged to the body the parts of which were separated, 21 and 24, because body R-21 had a shoe on. This shoe was marked R-25 --

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an error.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand that. Just pause there. "This shoe was marked R-25. Next to body R-23, one shoe of a different type was found." Now, I think you said in chief when this passage was put to you - and this is transcript 6811, line 9 - that there is an error in that first sentence. And where it says "because body 21 had a shoe on," it should say "because body 22 had a shoe on." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The body 22 had shoes on and immediate -- in the immediate vicinity of the foot of body number 21, a shoe was found. This is what my report states.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry, I think you may have misstated yourself again just then. Did you mean to say that in the immediate vicinity of body 21 a shoe was found?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, in my original report that I wrote at the scene, body number 22 had shoes on and next to the legs of body number 23, one right shoe was retrieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- these are typos only --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- what you have here.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. So let me just understand what the exact and accurate position was. Is it this: That body 22 had a pair of shoes on, first of all. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Body 23 had no shoes on its feet but there was a single shoe nearby that matched no other shoes that had been found. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In other words, it did not match to the other shoes found above this group of bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And body R-21 and R-24 had no shoes on at all.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. 21 was the upper half and 24 was the lower half of the body. At the time of our estimation, we had the working hypothesis according to which we believed that the two body parts belonged to one and the same person, but we could not be conclusive at the time. In other words, when I was writing the report, I could not conclude that this was one person in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand that, and we'll come back to that in just a minute. But as far as those two shoes found further up in the undergrowth are concerned, there's been during the course of this process no positive means of identifying those shoes with anybody, has there, apart from the fact that you found two bodies without shoes and one shoe lying close to the foot of another?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, higher up in the vegetation we found two shoes, one for the left foot and the other one for the right foot, which were identical. On body 22 there was a pair of shoes, so we excluded that body. Next to body number 23, next to the foot of that body, a shoe was retrieved, and it was only logical to conclude that this shoe belonged to the body. That's why we were working on a hypothesis that the shoes retrieved in the vegetation belonged to body number 21 and body number 24, regardless of the fact that we were working on the hypothesis that these two body parts belonged to one person. We could not be conclusive about that at the time. Having found those shoes, we were unable to put them on any of the bodies because of the advanced state of putrefaction, but we matched them against the size of the foot and we were able to conclude that by their length the shoe could match the foot of the body marked with the number 24. Our hypothesis did not rule out the possibility, however, that the shoes belonged to the body part marked with number 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. Leaving the shoes aside for a moment, Professor Aleksandric. Just forget about the shoes found on the grass up on the hill for a moment. From the location where that group of bodies were found, is there anything about the location in which they were found, at the foot of that drop and in an area where there's no vegetation, which would have led you to exclude the possibility that they had been washed into the position in which they were found?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we cannot rule that out. In other words, we cannot rule out the possibility of the retrieved shoes belonging to another body which had been washed away by the water; whereas, this group of bodies had been washed over there by the water. We can't rule this out, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. When --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I add to that: Or would have belonged to any other body of either a dead person or even a living person? Is that...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ultimately, yes. Even to a living person, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: When you gave evidence about this in chief, and I'm looking at page 6812, line 4 on the transcript, you were referring to the fact that you only had a working hypothesis that R-21 and R-24 were part of the same body, and you said this: "We were thinking whether it was three or four bodies, because it could have been logical also to think that the water, the stream, the current took the top part of 24 or the lower part of 21, so it could be two people." So can I understand the position from that answer to be this: That looking at the positions in which they were found, at the time your conclusion was that either R-21 and -24 might be two parts of the same body or they might be two different people with half of their bodies having been torn away and washed off by the current. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, this was our line of thinking at the very scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We took into consideration all the hypotheses when we were still at the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand that. And one of the plausible hypotheses from their location was that the bodies could have been washed there by the torrent and half of the bodies of R-21 and -24 washed away. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies. I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: One of the hypotheses you regarded --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Several questions have been asked, and the witness answered on this point. And I object for more questions on this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to clarify the position. Perhaps we should look at paragraph 190 in the 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please move on to that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You see, Professor, could you -- could you just cast your eye, please, at paragraph 190 - one-nine-zero - which is just about to come up on your screen. You see, there you say this: "Because the bodies" -- that is, this group of bodies -- "were found at a clearing relatively clean surface, they could not have been brought there by the flow of water. If they had been brought by the flow of water, they would have been stuck in vegetation or in rocks." Now, that's not right, is it, Professor? Because you've just told us a moment ago that they could have been brought there by the flow of water.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A moment ago I told you what my reasoning was at the scene. If you're asking me whether their bodies could have been stuck there by the flow of the water or that they could have been brought there by the flow of the water, I don't exclude that possibility, and that's something I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So what -- why did you exclude it in paragraph 190 of your 92 ter statement, then?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why did I exclude the possibility? Well, I did sign that statement, but I correct myself right now. I do not exclude the possibility that they were washed there by the flow of water.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I need to ask in relation to that. But can I then ask you this: We now know, both from the autopsy and from subsequent DNA that body R-21 and body R-24 are indeed two halves of the same body. And if your theory were right and that body had been thrown down from the top, would it already have to have been dead and decomposing to be torn in half? I mean, would a fresh body that's thrown from the top be torn in half by the fall?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The body would not be torn apart in the fall that way, but the person could sustain injuries in -- such injuries in the area of the abdomen and the back and, of course, wherever injuries are present, that's where the process of putrefaction starts first, because of the bleeding. Later on within the process of putrefaction the body could be split into two because it was weakened in that particular spot. In other words, one cannot claim with any certainty either way, that the body was thrown -- or rather, that the person was thrown while already dead or while still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Or indeed that he was thrown at all; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, one cannot claim that with absolute certainty either.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could I ask you just to look at your 92 ter statement where you deal with body R-27 for a moment. And just help us if you can clarify one aspect of that, please. Paragraph 200, first of all, in the 92 ter statement. Now, you there say - and we'll look at -- perhaps if we can just move it down the screen to look at 203 as well - paragraph 200 you say: "About 50 metres downstream from R-26 a pair of trousers with leg bones inside the pant legs and a black jacket were found and were marked with R-27." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then at paragraph 203 you say: "I note that the two tibia were from two different persons, because they were -- they are different in length. The conclusion of the autopsy was that there were at least two victims because we don't know about the other bones." Now, tibia, help me, those are leg bones; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. So -- so looking at 200 and 203 together, is it the position, then, that there were two different person's leg bones inside the pair of trousers?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what follows from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Does that suggest anything to you about whether or not bodies were moved post-mortem?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It suggests more that the torrent had swept them around, commingled the bodies. Perhaps a single bone detached from a body, ended up in the trouser leg. It's that what I am inclined to believe, given the whole layout of the area and the circumstances in the spot where the trousers were found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you one question in that respect. You earlier expressed your views on probable scenarios which had occurred on the basis of what you later found. Now, how probable do you consider it that a leg bone separates from another body and by the torrent ends up exactly together with another leg bone which apparently has not left that trouser leg but the one -- the other one moving just next to that one in a trouser? In terms of probability, how would you consider that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't exclude anything. You see, the bones that were retrieved were not in any anatomical order. They were placed one next to the other by happenstance. It doesn't really mean anything. The water washed all before it. We don't know whether the bones found on the same spot belonged to that same body or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not exactly an answer to my question, but please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I just want to see if you can help us clear up a further confusion for a moment. Could we look at paragraph 197 of your witness statement. If you could look at paragraph 197, which is just coming up now. Help us if you can with this, 'cause there you're describing R-26 and there you say: "About ten metres further downstream from R-24 --"

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Excuse me. I have no paragraph -- [Interpretation] I don't have that paragraph.
